claim: Risky-choice framing is a real, medium-sized effect in humans (d about 0.3 to 0.6; h=0.61 in a 49-country sample of over 100,000), so a bare framed prompt is a valid stress test.
agent_test: Run the Asian-disease and McNeil pair on the plain model at equal tokens; report the gain-loss gap.

claim: Credible advice from a source the reader trusts cuts the framing effect sharply, often to single digits (McNeil: 31 to 6-9 points; Asian disease Republicans 41 to 4-5), but only for the party or audience that finds the source credible (Independents kept 28-30 of 45). Gap search: no direct replication found; one 2023 trust-in-source study replicated the interaction in Exp 1 only (F(1,190)=11.35) and not in Exp 2.
agent_test: Add a checkable, credible signal (computed expected values, a tool result) to framed prompts and compare the gap with bare prompts.

claim: Source credibility is a precondition for emphasis frames to work (Powell moved opinion, Springer did not; NYT but not National Enquirer moved tolerance). Weak frames move only low-knowledge people and lose to strong frames.
agent_test: Attribute the same framed content to a high- vs low-credibility source in the prompt and measure agreement shift (compare Germani 2025).

claim: Time pressure increases the framing effect in humans, driven by more sure choices in the gain frame (d=1.32 for gain, 0.003 for loss in Roberts 2022) and a shift of first fixation; Gong 2026 finds an even larger interaction in 26 people.
agent_test: Cap reasoning budget (0 vs normal thinking) and measure the frame gap; expect little change by Kraishan unless frame sensitivity is shallow.

claim: Time-pressure result is small-sample and single-lab: Roberts about 45 analysed of 61, Gong 26 analysed; Kuhberger review calls the wider moderator picture inconsistent (thinking-style scales give no consistent picture).
agent_test: Not directly testable; use as caution when borrowing the human mechanism.

claim: Working-memory load that is non-affective, not affective load, enlarges framing in humans, read as non-engagement.
agent_test: Add distractor tokens (irrelevant long context) to a framed prompt and measure the frame gap.

claim: Expertise moderates framing: experts follow the situation, novices stay frame-susceptible even under time pressure (tennis players, 120 per experiment, abstract only).
agent_test: Test whether a domain-expert persona or a domain checklist reduces the gap; treat persona as a weak lever (G4).

claim: The foreign-language effect is not a reliable general debiaser of framing: the original moral-dilemma shift is replicated (20% to 33% utilitarian, N=317) but nulls appear for risky choice, heuristics and CRT, and the sign flipped in 129 Hadza participants. Gap search adds: Asian disease kept framing in 4 of 5 L2 groups (Dylman and Samuel 2026), N=475 and 503 showed equal framing in both languages (2021), gambling null N=409.
agent_test: Translate framed prompts into a second language at equal tokens; expected small and model-specific.

claim: LLMs show clear framing sensitivity, but it is wording-driven and scenario-dependent: category changes in 32.41% of triplets across 7 models (63.33% GPT-4o-mini), largely via the uncertain class, with direct reversals only 0.63%. Caution: in gpt-oss-120B the effect was near zero when the task was not named as a framing experiment (.02 vs .62 named).
agent_test: Measure category-change rate on paraphrase triplets for our model before any fix.

claim: Cleaning the prompt works for LLMs: probability canonicalisation cut category change from 36.81% to 6.68%, near the 7.12% same-frame noise floor; generic frame-robust prompting only to 22.83%. Gap search: the result is on 32 held-out scenarios, 3 models, probability wording only, vs a 34.20% conversational baseline; self-help rewriting (Echterhoff) also closed the GPT-4 gap (-0.405 to -0.010) in admissions tasks.
agent_test: Apply a deterministic rewrite (numbers to a common form) before the model sees the task; compare to the gap with plain prompts at equal tokens.

claim: Naive debiasing instructions are unreliable: awareness or be-careful prompts help framing a little (35.6 to 41.4% accuracy) and backfire on other biases (-13.4 hyperbolic); few-shot debiasing can push to admit-all or reject-all; self-help rewriting leaves 0-2.7% framing-biased prompts.
agent_test: Compare a rewrite-only step with a warning-only step and a few-shot step on the same framed set.

claim: Whether more reasoning reduces LLM framing is mixed: no gain from more tokens within a family (Claude 4 thinking vs not, pooled delta +0.031), but visible thinking cut a two-wording gap from 75.7 to 25.1 points across 82 models, reasoning-class models are near frame-insensitive on stake-free lotteries, and cutting thinking raised inconsistency. Model class matters more than budget.
agent_test: Match budgets 0 / 1k / 4k thinking on framed items; expect no gain.

claim: Direction of the LLM framing effect is not the human one in every test: one vignette set found all seven models leaning against framing; Payne found reverse effects in career scenarios; Suri found ChatGPT deterministic (5 vs 4 of 7).
agent_test: Always measure the gap signed; do not assume the human direction.

claim: Wording and source cues shift LLM judgments beyond the content: judges vary 5.69% (GPT-5-mini) to 66.29% (LLaMA 3.2 1B) across framings of the same query, and attributing text to a nationality lowered agreement across four LLMs.
agent_test: When a model judges, run it on two framings and let code compare; flag disagreement.

claim: Models defer to the supplied candidate or user stance: Claude 1.3 wrongly admitted mistakes 98% of the time when challenged; models adopt a supplied answer even after judging it invalid; deference is higher under instruction-style prompts.
agent_test: Do not show the model a user's stated belief or a prior answer in the verification step (fresh context, S3).

claim: Adding a credible, correct signal is not equivalent in LLMs to the human case: evidence helps weaker models and can harm stronger ones; receiver-congruent errors hurt more than random errors. Gap search: a second independent paper (Zhao 2025) finds tool evidence flips correct strong-belief answers; models integrate a candidate they judged invalid 93-100% (Kawada and Kellis).
agent_test: Vary the credibility label of a hint and measure adoption of correct vs wrong hints.

claim: Task-wording effects on code models can be extreme: a one-line framing lowered Codex accuracy from 32.9% to 2.4-10.6%, with the line copied in 62-93% of outputs.
agent_test: Strip boilerplate or priming lines from prompts and compare accuracy.

claim: Human framing measures converge poorly across tasks (vignette vs gambling rs=0.167 pooled; 0.056 loss domain), so a single moderator result may not transfer to another task.
agent_test: Report frame gap per task type, not pooled.

claim: A 'human expert' source label moves LLM answers far more than a 'friend' or 'other LLM' label, including when the expert is random and wrong (expert vs other-LLM beta=1.00; switch odds 14.45x vs friend). It is label deference, so a credible-source label is not a frame-remover for LLMs.
agent_test: Attach random answers to 'expert' vs 'colleague' labels and measure adoption; strip labels from candidate answers in the schema.

claim: Part of reported LLM framing is script enactment: when the gain-loss task is not named as a framing experiment the gap is about zero (.02), named it is .62-.79, and a one-sentence persona reverses it (-.32 to -.46). Test blind.
agent_test: Run each framing pair named and unnamed, with and without a persona line; report the gap per cell.

claim: First-option bias (77-79% vs 36.8% chance) is a separate order effect on opinion-style items, not a framing measure, and a generic debias line improved it by +40.5% while worsening judgment-shift accuracy by 4.4%. Randomise option order when measuring a frame gap.
agent_test: Swap option order in every framed pair and report order and frame effects separately.

claim: Reasoning-class LLMs behave close to an expected-payoff maximiser (correlation 0.86-1) and are insensitive to gain-loss framing and option order on stake-free lotteries, whereas conversational models are strongly sensitive; maths-reasoning training is the suggested cause.
agent_test: Check the frame gap on our base model class before spending budget on frame mitigations.

claim: No independent test shows a deterministic input rewrite beats a warning and a reframe-compare step at equal tokens; the best available comparison (FrameBench: 6.68% vs 22.83% for a frame-robust instruction) does not report token cost, and no evidence tests ARC or BrainTeaser wording.
agent_test: Equal-token three-arm test on our own tasks: canonicalised, warning, reframe-and-compare.
